input_text: Since I am unable to post reviews per dlc because it shows I didn't "buy" the dlc, I'll have to update my review for each DLC that comes out. DLC1: Combat engineer is really cool. It's nice being able to plop 6 turrets down and hold an area on your own almost. The campaign is horrible. 2nd mission in, I am fighting multiple mechs and a vehicle at once. Another time the enemy plops down a reaper turret that kills me in seconds. And this is in the beginning. Absolutely hating the campaign. So far, not worth the price. Definitely do not buy for the campaign, it basically gives everything to your enemy and kicks you in the nuts with it. DLC2: Psychics. Kind of a cool class with different powers. Telekinesis is not nearly as cool as it sounds, since you literally need cars and barrels in order to do damage, and the damage is not as much as some other classes' powers. So it is situational and not very strong. For the campaign: Unlike DLC1, you don't start off with a lot to work with. You begin with an extremely crappy class with barely any skills or slots to put them in. The first mission might as well of been called "Welcome to Dark Souls", and the 2nd mission literally threw multiple Hunters at me. With the super crappy beginning class. I did some save scumming and running like crazy to get past a few missions and can't seem to unlock anything good, so it has been even less fun than DLC1. DLC3: Weapon modding. I'm not sure it totally works for this kind of game, but it is cool none the less. There appears to be quite a few options, but there are not a lot of feasible ones; many options appear to be for niche builds. I do recommend getting this DLC if only to change the bullets of your main gun, so that it is more easy to cover armor pierce or energy stun. I've yet to do the campaign for this one, but until I update for that, just assume it is as bad as the other two or worse since that is the growing trend here. Overall: Each one adds something substantial to skirmish or multiplayer, but the campaigns are by far worse than the original.

input_text: Really excellent first-person shooter! At first, I didn't expect a lot from it, but I was very surprised. - an overall high quality VR shooter - although EA, I encountered no bugs at all - very entertaining and balanced gameplay - nice and fluid animation of the enemy soldiers and robots - wonderful retro 80s/Tron vibe - I love how the world seems to be build/un-build when you move through it - bullet-time never gets old + other fun power-ups - nice variety of levels - fantastic performance on a mid-range gaming laptop!! Recommended if you can appreciate a pure mindless shooter with a 80s arcade feel.

input_text: Another great puzzle coming from Sweety Cute Studio. Dances and Girls could just as well be named “Idol Girls” because they are all cast in a singing on colorfully lit stage environment. (Of course, except for the first 10 images the girls are not dressed much like you are likely to see in an idol performance!) The game setup is similar to Sweet and Cute, and the graphics are once again top quality—essentially art turned into puzzles. Play the game fullscreen to get the full impact. There are 10 girls with 4 levels of dress. The first 10 puzzles are quite easy, the next two sets of 10 are generally easy, and the last 10 puzzles are perhaps medium hard, but mostly just take more time because they have more pieces. With my puzzle-solving talent (or lack thereof), it took me a little over an hour and a half to complete them all. The game ran perfectly for me—no crashes, problems changing settings, and so on. There are 40 achievements. The puzzles are timed (no influence on the outcome), which for me provides additional replay value as well. Strongly recommended.

input_text: Buildings! Short, medium, and tall. One moment, your lance is leisurely crossing a street with no enemies in sight or even in radar contact. The next moment, enemy 'Mechs are firing atop or behind buildings! I think that in one particular mission, the enemy commander was even singing to me -- "Why do 'Mechs suddenly appear, every time you are near....cause just like me, they long to be, blasting you." But that was not all. That commander was likely laughing as I repeatedly missed hitting one of his lance mates that was firing from atop a building. However, I had the last laugh. All my missed shots hit the building instead. It collapsed (yes, the buildings can be destroyed!). So down went the unlucky 'Mech. The fall damage destroyed one leg and seriously damaged the other. But since excess leg damage transfer to a shoulder, there was damage there too. To add insult to injury, I destroyed the building in front of the enemy Catapult that was firing non-stop. So I was the one singing later, along that beach drinking song's tune (no shirt, no shoes, no problem song) -- "No building, no cover, no problem!" So here are the pros and cons of this DLC, based on the above and other experiences I have so far: Pros-- - new biome (urban city) - some new 'Mechs - some new equipment - if price is a non-issue, this DLC is fun even at full price Cons-- - for many, probably not worth the full price, so just wait until it goes on sale - really the urban setting is the best part of this DLC, with the destructible buildings and being able to expand your tactics because of it - some environmental effects could have been added, like the sound of traffic and stuff - understandable but not quite realistic that the hustle and bustle of the city suddenly totally stops just because your team went stomping in, with some passing civilian vehicle or two possibly enhancing the experience of possible civilians being in harm's way In conclusion: - this DLC is worth getting - the urban setting biome alone is worth it since it is quite the departure from lonely biomes in the standard game - though not realistic, it is understandable why the city suddenly feels like it is frozen in time, since the software developers made all buildings destructible and any additional detail would likely have slowed the game

input_text: Review date: 5/4/22 (Early Access) I really, really, really want to give this game a good review. I do. I just can't do it. YET. My recommendation is to wait until this gets fleshed out a bit more. It's VERY early access, but has a LOT of potential. Unlike some other dragon games I've seen, this one is quite playable. It's just not ready yet. Good stuff about this game: You are a DRAGON! The dragon you play is absolutely adorable. I enjoyed playing this character. You can indeed FLY! Breath weapon is DEVASTATING (as it should be ;) ). Relatively bug-free (nothing that prevented playing, or caused issues playing at least). Graphics are nice, if dark. Now, the bad stuff: Flight burns stamina. Your stamina drains fast, and refills slow. Forget about flying all over and doing devastating air strikes. You don't have the stamina to fly very far at all. Nor can you swim: you basically run across the bottom of the water. Whoops (that's probably just an EA issue). Add to that: melee attacks use stamina. One melee strike uses up almost 70% of your stamina. In other words, you can strike ONCE. OR fly. Forget about flying in and striking. In fact, forget about using melee at all, as one strike didn't kill the first creatures you fight (your breath weapon does, and recharges fast, so it's really your only weapon choice). Melee and stamina need to be tweaked (unless there are possible upgrades later, which I didn't see). If I am blowing through almost all my stamina with one swing, there better not be anything left in front of me afterwards! But there is, so it's kinda balanced wrong. The only way to STOP flying is to fly into the ground (which is kinda clumsy), or run out of stamina (which happens pretty quickly, actually). There should be a button to drop out of flight. If there is one, I didn't find it--it's not the obvious choice of the same button that start flight. The game scenery has all been dark. Not sure if that's the theme the are going for, but having some brighter colors/areas (in town, no less) would be better. I completed the first quest, and am told to return to the quest giver. I have no clue where he is, nor a marker to find him. Wasting a lot of time running around looking for him. There were markers for the bad guys, where's my quest marker to go back? The game says you can cast spells, however, none of those keybinds are working--I tried, when I discovered the hard way how bad the melee attack was--they should be hotkeys 1-5 (or something like that). Nothing happened with any of those. Or they also use the perpetually-drained stamina. However, it's possible I haven't unlocked them yet, as I only did one quest. I may have more feedback as I play more (assuming I ever find that questgiver). I would really love to see a few updates to this, and change my review. For now though... I recommend waiting and see where it develops.

input_text: I LOVE FISTI-FLUFFS!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! It's such a cute game, I love all of the cats and their cute little cat sounds. It's easy to tell which cat you are playing as, even when the stages get a little chaotic, and the ability to give them little outfits and glasses just makes them more endearing. I probably like the destruction mode the best, but kibble defense is also pretty high up there and gets pretty challenging the longer you play! There are a few different game modes, all of which are pretty basic and easy to pick up (especially for someone like me that tends to have to relearn all the buttons each time I jump back into a game). If you like cats, silliness, and chaos, I highly recommend this game! The stages are really unique and I love trying to get the powerups for my cats! Some modes definitely feel a bit harder than others, but I think that helps the game feel balanced as you can't win any specific game mode effortlessly. The game is still fun even when I am not "good" at a game mode, it doesn't feel disheartening or frustrating at all. I like getting the unlockable items even though I tend to gravitate back to the same ones each time regardless of which cat I am playing as (lol). The $20 cost might seem steep at first, but honestly I think it's a no-brainer kind of investment. The game has so much going for it, and I am happy to support the developers for basically the same price as a pizza. tldr: Fisti-Fluffs rules! It's not a perfect game but it's got heart and (most importantly) cute kitties. In short, I love it.

input_text: TL;DR: the negative experiences people have with this locomotive are likely due to a lack of clarity in the manual, which I explain in the review. For the price that I paid, I'd say this DLC is a good addition to your collection (actual review begins below). I've noticed that many of the negative reviews for this locomotive seem to focus on one of two things: not being able to move or poor steaming quality. What needs to be remembered is that this is a Pro Range locomotive, and it simulates operating procedures much more realistically than most other Train Simulator locomotives. A large portion of the locomotives in this simulator have the braking functions operated entirely by one set of controls; that is, the train brake lever (the lever on the right in the F4 HUD). However, the Manor (and most other Pro Range locomotives) rely on both the main train brake lever as well as the small ejector to have the brakes function properly. This is why the locomotive won't move for some people; after putting the train brake lever in the release position, you also have to turn the small ejector on ("J" key by default). Once you do this, the brakes will release successfully. Interestingly, the steaming problems that reviewers mention is also caused by misusing the small ejector. In order to create a vaccum to release the brakes, the small ejector uses a lot of steam. When stationary or running light at low speeds, this isn't much of an issue as the locomotive's steam production can usually keep up with this usage. However, once you begin pulling a train at speed, your boiler pressure will drop fast. This is because you have to turn off the small ejector (also the "J" key as it's a toggle control) once you're moving at about 5-10mph. Don't worry, the brakes will remain released after turning it off. Other things that will help boost steam production are opening the dampers (holding the "M" key by default) and closing the cylinder cocks after leaving them open for a few seconds after starting ("C" key by default). Normally, this would likely be an issue of not reading the manual, especially with the Pro Range DLC as most of the ones that I've bought cover this aspect of operation. The thing is, none of this is mentioned anywhere in the manual for this DLC (with the exception of the key controls, of course), which I personally think is a major issue. This is especially the case for someone who's new to the Pro Range and not familiar with these realistic operating procedures. If it weren't for this major oversight, I'm sure this DLC wouldn't have gotten such a negative reception. If there's anything that should be fixed on this locomotive, it's the inclusion of this vital operating aspect in the manual besides a simple keyboard control. As for the DLC itself, I find it to be a decent addition to one's collection. Not the best, but certainly far from the worst. The controls are definitely more advanced than your typical Train Simulator locomotive, and I recommend that anyone driving this (or any Pro Range locomotive, for that matter) use the F5 HUD. The inclusion of Mk. 1 coaches is always nice, and though I haven't finished all of them yet, the two scenarios I've done so far have worked just fine and were enjoyable. However, it definitely looks a bit dated. As someone else mentioned, this actual addon was created by JustTrains in 2013 and was likely re-released under the Pro Range in 2020. The locomotive's appearance definitely shows its age; it was probably good at the time, but it simply doesn't hold a candle to the much higher-fidelity models produced for Train Simulator these days. On top of that, I must also agree with other reviewers on the physics: for a Pro Range locomotive, they're not great. They're better than most standard locomotives in the simulator, but they fall short in terms of realism compared to other Pro Range locomotives I've driven. Additionally, some of the controls are simplified compared to their real life counterparts (e.g. the injectors require no adjustment whatsoever to get water into the boiler, they function more like on/off switches). So where does this DLC sit, exactly? Personally, disregarding the issue with the manual, I think it serves as a good introduction to the Pro Range for someone who may be new to it. This DLC allows someone to experience the more advanced control schemes offered by the Pro Range without the added factor of hyper-realistic physics (which may be seen as a positive or negative depending on who you ask). Would I recommend this DLC? Well, that depends. First of all, I would never buy this for its full price (though I'd say the same about almost every other Train Simulator DLC pack, so take that with a grain of salt). However, for the sale price of $11.99 (what I paid), it's a different story. If you're someone like me whose equally content driving Pro Range engines with realistic physics as well as standard locomotives with basic physics, I'd say this DLC is worth it. For $12 you get a decent quality (but somewhat dated) locomotive in a few liveries, some coaches, and four standard scenarios for the S&DJR. Not the best deal in the world, but certainly not a bad one in my opinion. If you're someone whose new to the Pro Range, I'd still recommend it. It's a great way to get used to the more advanced controls without having to go all-in with hyper-realistic physics (though I do believe that some Pro Range locomotives allow for simplified physics, so this may be a moot point). Just make sure you remember the details about the small ejector I mentioned above (read the manual, too)! However, if you're someone who’s only looking for top-notch, highly detailed, and hyper-realistic DLC, then you should probably look elsewhere. Overall, for $11.99, I'd recommend it, but not as strongly as some of the other DLC packs available for Train Simulator.

input_text: I remember playing the first R-Type Final, developing the OF line, wishing they would eventually get a powerful Wave Cannon. That dream is finally realized, albeit in the form of paid DLC. I wouldn't buy this at full price, but I paid 4.19 USD and I feel like I got my money's worth. First, you get a ship with Standard Wave Cannon III and the ability to switch to a few other Standard Wave Cannons, the "OF Force -" and the capability to switch to any of the other OF series' Forces, and a Purple Pod that fires two shots at about 30 degree angles which can be switched out for other colored Pods in the OF series. The Purple Pod also launches out a bit when you press the Force Detach button. Second, you get free resources in the shop--they'll be listed with the name MARIKO, which will help you develop other cool ships, especially early on. Lastly, you get a pilot helmet and suit that increases the amount of resources you gain a bit, albeit at the cost of a reduction in Pilot Points. Getting this DLC seems to make the entire rest of the OF line obsolete, so combined with the ship itself, the resources in the in-game store, the resources obtained from the suit, and allowing you to put off the OF fighter line until you're doing it to unlock every ship, you're getting some value with this DLC. The ship itself is also very good for beginners who are struggling with the antiquated ships they give you at the start of the game, and since you need to beat levels for resources, this might be a good early pickup for beginners as well. Although, I would suggest trying out the free DLC "April Fool's Prototype" first and seeing if you can get through the game in that. Overpriced, get on sale, good for beginners, actually a pretty cool ship.

input_text: This is a good puzzle game with a very strange story. If you prefer casual puzzle games (like me) over hardcore puzzle games, don't be put off by the comments! It's really not as hard as they're making it sound. There is one part where everyone, myself included, gets stuck (the first statue puzzle in the sewers), but it's not the difficulty of the puzzle that's hard, it's figuring out where the sequence begins. Once you know that, it's just another average puzzle. All the other puzzles just require simple logic or solving fairly easy riddles. The music in the Ghost Coast section is very nice. I really enjoyed that. I also really appreciate the speed at which you can speed walk. You're able to run from one place to the next rather than slowly plodding along. In a couple areas where you need to cover a little distance, this is extremely useful. So this is definitely a fantasy puzzle game rather than a walking simulator. I also love that, even though the game has been out for a couple years, the dev is still actively involved in answering questions, responding to comments, and is thinking about adding a patch to the game. He's also very friendly. Everything works as it should, and there are no bugs, which is fantastic. I'm quite pleased with this game. It's relatively short (only 4 levels), but there are two different endings. The puzzles are hard enough to make you feel satisfied when you solve them, but they're not so hard that you want to quit... unless you're that one other reviewer who rage quit lol. It's fun, and really, that's all you can ask for from a game.

input_text: Edge of War is a tactical, turn-based, (medium) fantasy CRPG. Though, currently there is very little story and little in the way of character development outside of stat and skill choices. All of these are within expectations of a standard issue isometric CRPG. Classics like Persuasion, Stealth and Lore skills currently find very little use, though. The main focus for the current build is combat. The only exception would be Mechanics (lockpicking), which is essential to get the best possible loot. And there is plenty to be found! The setting is somewhat unique among CRPGs as it is apparently based on Finnish folk lore. You will still fight bandits and wolfs. But you will also learn, that Skyrim's trolls are a far cry, of what a troll can truly be. A 10m rock-skinned behemoth, whose scream alone can induce fear into your characters. In the background, and surely part of a narrative to come, is what appears to be an ancient, way more advanced civilization than the current medieval-ish one. Spirit energy (vaeki), a form of usable magic for your characters, based constructs will likely appear eventually, think robot soldiers. Part of one of your missions is to inspect parts of such a construct. I am very hopeful for more here! Noteworthy also are the 2 races that accompany the humans: Hirwio (moose headed humanoids) and Peyko (a mix between an ugly witch and a goblin, still human sized), both of which specialize, where humans are generalists. This is important as you are not supposed to be able to max out everything. Overall it's a bit of a fresh wind, though not too out there. The by far most interesting part about this game is the partial procedural generation of the world. I believe this is a great innovation and improvement on any not too narrative focused RPG. It allows for slight but relevant changes to every playthrough: other enemies, different loot, other special characters, other quest locations, other shops. I am currently on my 4th playthrough and can say that each felt significantly differentiated from the others. On full release this system alone will give this game an insane amount of replay value! As implemented as it is now, I would already view it as a tool worth revisiting for any CRPG developer. For example Pathfinder WotR with this kind system in place might have hooked me way beyond 500 hours (200 hours currently). I believe it is that essential! Lastly, there is the current technical state of the game: It is suprisingly stable and works almost without issues! There are some minor bugs and annoyances to be expected from early access. None of which were substantial or couldn't be remedied with a quick load. Autosave is already implemented and works perfectly fine! I suffered 1 single crash. The developers, a team currently mostly privately developing the game, is also aware of most of these bugs and answers regularly on Steam discussions. There is also a discord for further discussions. Overall I can recommend the game wholeheartedly, even if it's relativley short (per playthrough) at this point. This may just be a true diamond in the rough. I have high hopes for further developments!

input_text: Platformer game from Hentai Room. Does it deserve the negative rating it has? As a magic practitioner, Sofiya, you venture into dungeons and cemetaries to discover the history behind your clan's rules. As you progress through the 45 dungeons, you will find books revealing bits of the story, but don't expect much here; the explanations are vague and way too brief. There is only one ending, and you can rather easily find all of the books, so one playthrough is sufficient to see everything. The focus was placed on the platforming parts. Ok, I get it. The moving pace feels very sluggish in comparison to similar titles, but it is not as detrimental to the gameplay as other reviews describe it. I won't count it as negative. It is what it is, and I got used to it shortly after starting. Aside from platforming, you also have various enemies to deal with. You have only one basic attack and three special ones to fight them. There is not much variety here, even considering that it is a budget title. After a few hits, most enemies will wave a white flag for a moment. You can then activate the sex finisher to eliminate them. This takes a few seconds and can't be skipped, so the pace suffers. However, with the double jump, you can avoid most enemies, so you don't need to kill them all. Especially since you don't gain experience from fighting, just recovery items and special shots. The main difficulty of this game is the platforming aspect. Most spikes are one hit k.o., and there are no checkpoints, but the levels are very short, so I don't feel like checkpoints are necessary in the first place. I certainly did not struggle much to complete levels, and I managed to clear most without any deaths. It is not a precision platformer, so I don't get why people cry about the difficulty. I'm certainly not a pro at platforming. Similarly, the three boss fights are pretty basic and easy to win. Next, I need to mention some negatives. Despite being a short, budget title, the lack of creativity is evident. There is very little variety of enemies, levels feel samey, and there is no character progression. Even at this low price, I expected a bit more. I can't say I hated playing it, but I was not very amused either. To the developer's defence, I believe it is the first platformer game he has made, so perfection is not expected. Still, more could've been done. I rate the experience as neutral. The pixel art is somewhat below average. The finisher animations lack polish and quality but are fluid enough to see what is happening. Sadly, there is little variety of scenes. Dungeons lack creativity as well. Some are way too short, and others feel too bland. Certainly, more work could be put into their creation. The visuals are slightly below my expectations as well. The music is pretty simple but mostly fits the theme. Nothing really stands out, but nothing sounded annoying either. Just good enough. The sound effects are a bit lacking, though. No bugs encountered, but on one of the levels, I fell on spikes that did not kill me. Rather insignificant glitch. Overall, a very simplistic platformer with some sexy pixel art and okay music. Even for a budget title, it all feels a bit uninspired and repetitive. I find it hard to recommend this game, but my actual rating would be neutral. It's certainly not the worst I've seen, but more effort should've been put into the development. 4.6/10

input_text: My Experience I'm often drawn to stealth games, especially when I'm given clear information on what enemies can perceive. Although it's clearly a budget title, the trailer and screenshots for Heist Master led me to believe that it could provide this type of information. And honestly, it does - it's clear when you're in an enemy view cone (the cone turns red), how far the sound travels when you step on a metal floor or shatter glass, and when you're hidden by smoke and can remain safe from enemies or automated turrets. Your thief can dispatch enemies quickly with attacks from behind, and can don costumes that allow him to traverse certain areas without detection (for a limited period of time - these costumes seem to disintegrate after a period of time for some reason). I was generally able to complete the levels quickly, especially when the four-digit passcodes and keys are so clearly visible in the game's isometric perspective. Within each set of levels you can purchase upgrades from time to time to enhance your thief or reduce the effectiveness of enemies or cameras in the levels that remain in the set. I would usually purchase some of these (I didn't know what else to do with my money), but I wouldn't call them necessary for success. Although the game was cheap, I still found myself wanting more cohesive and substantial content from it. I played sets of levels in a variety of locations (the casino that you see in the trailer has nine levels), and it felt as though these levels were randomly pulled from a bag. As I played, both locations and levels seemed to be repeated. After a while, I found myself just trying to unlock all of the characters, since the game provided me with no larger-scale goal. The last character I could unlock was Spider-man, but unlocking him required completing randomized sets of challenges. One of these challenges was using a zipline a certain number of times. It was easy to use ziplines, since your thief is essentially required to use them for basic traversal in various levels. However, the game seemed to be randomly pulling together levels that included no ziplines, so I was unable to complete this challenge. This was the final blow for me in terms of spending more time with the game. Heist Master is generally bug-free and is solid mechanically, but really seems more like a demo than a full game. I'd be interested to see developer SoupInIt Games put together a game using these mechanics that actually has a story or an arc to it.

input_text: First, I want to point out that a lot of people are complaining about poor translation. I have played the game thoroughly and, for the most part, it is properly translated. It starts to get iffy toward the end but it's bearable. I think many players may be confusing translation with 1st and 3rd person writing. In this game, it switches between both and the only indication is the lack of a name for the speaker. This applies to Irell as well as the Princesses so it can get confusing rather quickly. The writting format is pretty basic but enough to get descriptions and thoughts across. There's a heavy focus on how Irell Reis feels about every little thing. Some dialogue gets repeated despite already encountering it based on who you are following, ect. Probably about half of the dialogue boxes should be merged together or removed entirely to reduce redunancy. The game would do a lot better overall just by enhancing the dialogue to make it more relevant. It would also be more believable and immersive if the vocabulary wasn't juvenile and overused; ex: "cute", "plebian" and nobility titles. I would like to see the game revised this way in the future, or have their next game written more eloquently. Some of the voices sound like they were recorded at a low quality. Personally, I listen to the first few lines of a character and then turn it off. Most of them sound identical aside from tone. I enjoy imagining their voices on my own, with or without the tone implied by the creator. It's very difficult to know who you've picked to follow or how to continue to properly follow them without a lot of trial-and-error, unless you use one of the player made guides. There's a few on Steam that work well. I recommend using the Story Line portions first. After that, you can replay the game to get any of the Achievements missed. Holding the space bar down will rush through all of the dialogue. It should only take a few minutes to get them this way so definitely enjoy the story line first. Most of what you read is based on original lore and backstory for the characters. Once you've triggered an ending there is a -lot- of reading. You will need to get every ending to learn every characters story as only a few interact per play through. Also, keep in mind that not all of the character stories are updated at the same time. Each ending varies in length. One of them was a good 3 hours of reading after the choices ran out. I didn't expect this as it was my first playthrough so it quickly became a case of "when is this going to end?" for 2 of those 3 hours. If you like plot twists, and the ones in this game can get ridiculous, as well as learning about characters then it will keep you playing until the end. Fair warning, it gets ridiculous. The artwork, for some of the characters, was very well done. I would have liked to have seen more stills of events, especially during major scenes and Dyanna's finale. It would have made the bloated dialogue more bearable and the story more immersive overall. The UI needs some work. All of the options in the menu takes a little bit longer than normal to load and usually feels like the game hasn't registered the request. By the time I move the mouse over and click the option a second time it loads. The Quick Save & Quick Load options are not explained. You can only manually save or load during dialogue where it is listed to the right. [Having now completed the game, I will say that overall it has a low quality plotline from character to character. Personality preference will determine how much you enjoy the game. If you get bored with a character, I recommend either holding space bar and finishing to get the achievements or drop them entirely and move on to someone else.] It's worth it at 50% off, plus free DLC. 6.5/10 could be a potential 8/10 as a VN with polishing I recommended.

input_text: When I saw the videos and description of Ravenmark, I thought I had stumbled on another hidden gem like Valkyria Chronicles. Alas, there are not much hidden gems and most times you will just pick up another little pebble. Ravenmark is such a disapointment that looked good at first glance. A warning should have been the fact that Ravenmark is an iOS port. While that doesn't mean that it automatically has to be a bad game, there are still some implications that come along with it. Games for portable devices almost always don't want to bother the player with decisions that he made in earlier stages of the game. Concerning an RPG or strategy game, this effectively means that there are most likely no player choices to be made like specialising the skills of your units, upgrade units after a battle and carry it over to the next or RPG-choices that affect the course of the story. In short, you can expect that everything that adds salt and pepper to a RPG or strategy game will be left out. This, sadly, is the case with Ravenmark. The following list rates the different aspects of the game using a scale from very bad (---) to very good (+++): Stability/Bugs: +++ No bugs or stability issues encountered. Good job. RPG-aspects: - The story is a railroad slideshow without any interaction or possibility to make choices by the player. The characters are flat and either unmotivated good, bad and/or naive. Sometimes there's a voice narration of the character's conversations, which is nice. Tactical aspects: + You can give direct commands only to a maximum of six units during any given turn, while you will have at most times more than six units of yours on the battlefield. You can group units together and these new formations can be commanded with only a single command. Unfortunately, formations will often times not do or will not be able to do what you've ordered them to. All in all the tactical aspects are okay and the formation system adds a nice new idea to the genre. Strategic-aspects: --- There are simply no strategic decisions to be made. You can't upgrade units or characters, you can't decide which units to bring into battle, you can't decide on which terrain to fight, you have no choices regarding infrastructure, unit supply, economics or whatsoever. Price: - Considering the fact, that this is an iOS port, 15 € comes pretty close to a rip-off. With the lack of RPG-decisions and no strategic value, Ravenmark comes down to a casual game with some boring slideshow story. Honestly said, I wouldn't want to pay money for that no matter the cost.

input_text: I don't remember hearing about Vellum anywhere before Steam pushed it to my recommendations, citing Roboquest as a similar title. It's a highly-competently-designed third-person roguelite shooter with a surprising amount of quality of life features and little cosmetic flourishes, some you might not even find in other quality examples of roguelite shooters. It's got up to four player coop, which you won't find in Roboquest (limited to 2 player) or Ziggurat 2, Immortal Redneck or Battle Shapers (No coop whatsoever). It's got the ability to reconnect to a multiplayer run in progress if you get dropped, which I haven't seen in ANY coop roguelites. Vellum casts the players as wizards of pen and ink, the Scribes of an endless magical library, whose tomes are gateways to worlds of fiction brought to life, but are threatened by dark creatures known as the Torn. The tomes kept in this libary act as the various rogue runs, each with unique gameplay mutators. A choice of ink color acts as your character class, providing passive abilities and modifiers to your choice of primary and secondary spells- one generates mana, and the other consumes it. Combat is of the type of rogue that I prefer, where it is balanced around your character frequently taking damage and offering various means to mitigate this- regenerating shields, stacks of damage resistance called "Varnish", the red ink class's lifesteal mechanic, etc. The library itself acts as a playable hub area in the vein of the Space Rig in Deep Rock Galactic or the Basecamp in Roboquest. Here you can find stations to change your equipped ink color or spells, and upgrade your "ink level", unlocking new passive buffs and perks, called "inscriptions." Customizing the appearance of your Scribe is also possible, with different helmets, robes, spellbooks and back accessories. Completing new tomes for the first time unlocks various features and interactables around the library, such as target dummies to gauge your damage output. There's even a nook set aside for each player to customize with decorations like furniture, paintings and the like. The commitment to the literary theme runs deep, with most mechanics, enemies and other elements having some kind of literary term to denote them- Enemy groups include Splices, Tangents and Ravings, the requisite roguelike perks are called "Pages", The yellow ink class has a critical hit mechanic referred to as "Flourish", the blue ink class has damage-over-time effects referred to as "Blot", you can get a bonus for using a specific spell and/or playing a specific tome called "Suggested Reading," and so on. These terms are almost always explained adequately and an in-game help text is available for, *ahem*, further reading. Additional mutators, called "Bindings", can be selected before a run, offering increased combat difficulty but commeasurately increased rewards of Quillmarks and Guild coins. The former is used for purchasing new spells, inks and upgrades, while the latter is for cosmetic purchases such as helmets, robes and furnishings for your nook. There are of course, no microtransactions, but who would put those in a roguelite? Uniquely, Vellum also offers endgame raid dungeons in the various Torn realms, which as of this writing I have only scratched the surface of. Much like an actual MMO raid, they appear to require a degree of team coordination much higher then the more casual tome runs. Vellum is stylish and fun to play and I highly recommend it to any fans of shooters or action roguelites.

input_text: I enjoyed the game far more than I thought I would. Though i'd really call it more of a visual novel than a game, but the gameplay and choices are already better than most visual novel games out there in my opinion. In this game, YOU are the Sleeper, you are expected to self-insert. Make the choices YOU would make, consequences be damned, but above all, survive. Something about this game and how it played, and how it was written, and choices it allowed you to make just kept me hooked. The hours played (at this time, 12) reflects one entire playthrough of both the base game + free DLC. And I enjoyed every bit of it. The first few "cycles" as they are called in this game, can be brutal if you don't prepare for it. Once you get past the rather oppressive early game (which is very thematically fitting and would not have as much impact on the game if it were not there), this game carries itself extremely well. However, It doesn't take much for your character to go from barely surviving, to thriving, and being incredibly resource rich. While this is also fitting in a way, it also kinda detracts from the experience a bit, as halfway through the game, I pretty much stopped worrying about every experiencing a "game over" and stopped worrying about my "condition". However, by the time I became "overpowered", the story had me hooked, and I was already happily on my way to finish the story and decide my fate. I got this game on sale and it was more than worth it. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a fair bit of reading in an engaging way, and with a game that makes your choices matter, encouraging you to press on.

input_text: So I will give the game a very minor recommendation. The games graphics are quite good; the organs look good however I wish there was more detail. The environments look good but I felt were underutilized. Excellent voice acting, I really felt all the actors were putting effort into their roles. Whether it was the disinterested security guard or the main character, trying to maintain his professional composure while clearly harboring some deep mental problems. I will try give my observations of the game while avoiding spoilers. This game has potential but it fumbles what could be something very interesting. The medical language used in the game clearly shows the devs did their homework on this on the nature and process of preforming an autopsy. The bodies in the story I felt were well designed, however that ends when going to autopsy only mode. The observations are all randomized but they use the same male and female models every time, which is a shame because I know the devs know how to make detailed models but those are only in the story. the story is also quite linear with virtually no deviations. I will admit the secret ending surprised me but it wasn't exactly shocking and I got it without even knowing that it was the secret ending. The game's story is short, you can finish it in one sitting with no problems. Technically it runs fine, never crashed on me and there weren't any glitches [that I could find]. However, some of the minigames were a bit frustrating; it requires precise movements and when cutting certain things, if you are even one pixel off then it won't register complete. In the end, I feel if this were a longer game with more story and character development then I feel like it would be much better and I believe the autopsy only mode is a missed opportunity with how they designed it. So I would not recommend this game at full price but I don't think this is a bad game per say, a good foundation but with not enough content to take advantage of it. I don't know the full intentions of the devs but I feel like if they had more time with this game before releasing it they could have made a much better game. So while I like it, I can completely understand why others don't. TLDR: Not a bad game but wait for a sale.

input_text: I recommend the game but please read the long review. In this game leveling up is easy. But quite grindy to maintain that upped level properly. This is a really cute game AND equally tough to manage lol.. 😂 I request to DEVs please don't get me wrong. The game is honestly cute. I love all characters walking around, lively city, shops to buy ingredients, the graphics style, recent HUGE and FREE bakery update, Just because of this cuteness and my love for cooking games made me buy it even though I knew I'll never be good at this game. 😅 This game is solely for multiplayer. Solo players like me will look for a moment to breathe if gone wrong. Customer patience meter is low and food servings available in one cook is low as well. So when your restaurant is gaining fame, customers will come in more. Each of them won't have much patience, the food servings will end in a blink. But before you can cook the next serving -- your customer will rush out in anger. 😡 There's no setting available to turn up the patience meter longer or increase the servings number. So a solo player is never able to offer more than 2/3 recipes in their restaurant menu .🙄 The cooking process is not very easy as well. You'll level up soon but you gonna need couple practice cooks to offer servings after servings to your customers without loosing them. Ingredients will run out quickly. Every ingredient needs extra step to be prepared to use in the cooking/garnishing which is realistic I'd say. It's very easy to make mistakes during cooking if you're not paying attention. And throwing away food will decrease your ingredients quickly. In the middle of rush hour -- you'll find you're out of ingredients. You gotta wash your plates too or you will run out of plates to serve customers. Another and again another hurdle! 😭 Don't worry. There are some perks you can unlock to mildly help yourself, not much though. There's a Free mode too but it's a little odd. It's not like you're able to run a restaurant in free mode. input_text: A great sequel to Persona 5. Some of the characters who were mostly on the sideline in the original story have new story arcs, *cough cough* Haru, and the story is overall great. The jails in all the different locations are unique and they'er different enough from the palaces to stand out, but some of them are way too short (Kyoto and Okinawa especially). The soundtrack is amazing, some of the jail themes are insanely good (Anti Hero and Counterfeit Phantom are my personal favourites) and the gameplay is really fun. It's about what you'd expect from a Persona hack and slash, all the characters have differing combos, weapons and ways to play them (for example skull can charge his special attacks to make them hit harder and fox is more about throwing a bunch of hits quickly), the thing i personally liked was that every one of joker's personas changes his showtime animation a bit and they also change some of his combos a little. Now the glaring issue with this game, the performance, this game can't handle newer multicore cpus for some reason, you might even experience crashes alongside the ridiculous frame drops, BUT using Process Lasso and setting it to performance mode and giving it usage over all cores, P and E alike, might remedy it. Personally for me after I used it, the performance went back to what I would've expected, no frame drops, always 60 fps and most importantly NO CRASHES! Also the Digital Deluxe edition and 2 DLC packs aren't worth it, you already get enough items from playing the game and the legacy bgm is cool but not worth 10 Euro.

input_text: First impressions: Extremely polished and bug-free for an early access release. The same good ol' D**mRL action. (Let's all take a moment of silence to extend a gigantic middle finger to Bethesda/Zenimax lawyers for going after that wonderful fan project.) But the dungeon changed. I didn't encounter an equivalent of the stairs to Hell's Arena in my run, so I dunno if the dungeon is a reskin and we can expect to encounter familiar places under a new name, or if it's a complete redesign. Redesign is better I guess, to get brand new content to play, since we can still download and play DRL, which is even getting new updates thanks to this game. I know most monsters are simply reskinned from D**mRL with the same mechanics, but I find the new sprites, sound and names well-chosen. Not knowing the capacities of a new, large enemy was really scary again, good job there. Some enemies also have variants (frost, poison) which I don't remember from the predecessor game. Perks have been reworked, for instance Reloader lvl2 is more powerful than lvl1 now, and lvl 3 has the effect from the previously separate "Shottyman" perk that depended on lvl2. One major, welcome convenience is that weapons that drop from enemies are always empty of ammo. Gone is the compulsive alterning between the G (pick up) and U (unload) keys to make sure you loot every bit of ammo on the map to make sure you don't penalize yourself. This is one instance where I'll take gameplay over "realism". If you're coming to this from Jupiter Hell and not D**mRL, prepare to enjoy the various liquid floors (water, acid, lava) and the destructible walls, they add so much to the atmosphere. I have some minor gripes with the UI (such as the one for modding weapons) which takes too many clicks and keystrokes to perform some actions, and makes it hard to compare weapons properly. Also, level generation is sometimes not that great, cutting off sections behind large bodies of acid or lava, which are very expensive to cross, and placing teleporters and levers that are too dangerous to be worth trying. Eventually, you'll figure out ways to deal with it, but those situations will always drain your resources, sometimes for nothing in return. (BTW, if you never experienced the original DRL, it's free, you can download it from chaosforge, or even easier, get the DRL mod for this game from the Steam Workshop.)

input_text: Game idea shortly is to get the key and reach the next level and find collectables while rolling around in a marble that is affected by gravity but depending on level has one or more forms it can take to use abilities that are needed to solve the level. Abilities can be light form, floating form, fire form or metal form. Noteworthy is also that the controllable marble ball is not a flipper ball that gets thrown around helplessly - instead the player has pretty good control over the ball plus ability to execute double or even triple jumps if executed correctly. This results in the player jumping around pretty nimbly from one ledge to another yet evey now and then there are places where you need to do precise jumping - and the control over the marble ball allows the player to do just that. Rest be assured though if hard platformer games are not your tea as on average this game is more casual and based on overall mood rather than a true skill requiring game. Level design is simple but good enough. Mostly ice caves, fire caves etc with switches and collectables. Light is important in every level as you need to be able to see where you are going. Sometimes you need to flick switches to be able to see properly. Soundtrack can be very moody or epic. Certain songs reming me of Two Steps from Hell which is not a bad thing at all. And how does this game compare to some other titles? Marble Mayhem: Fragile Ball it is not. This does not require that much raw skill although certain levels may frustrate younger players. Collisions and Nightsky -games are closer but this game has more control and does not get as frustrating. but may loose on better level design and challenge if that is what you want. Game is mostly bug free. Only noticed a bug in the options menu where you tried to use both pad and mouse. it seems to confuse the game but it's easily overcome by using the mouse. Also a con i can think of is the lack of lore or proper in-game explanation on what you are doing and where you are going. Game got the nice soundtrack so some spoken dialog or even text would have helped. Lacking details where there should be some would be perhaps the best explanation here. I got this game for -50% but it's easily worth full price and for me the best purchase during this dreadful steam sale. Try it out. As long as you are able to get over the few slow levels early on then this game will start to shine quite quickly.

input_text: I really wanted to love it... (minor spoilers) Okay, so this is more of an expansion of the first game rather then a DLC which isn't a bad thing, but there are some issues I had with it. I will start with the positive: Gameplay was fun and I like the new enemies and takedown attacks you can use. The new cryo weapon takes a little bit to get used to but is fun to mess with once you get it. Game never crashed on me. The cons: Performance issues - I'll keep it short. Bad stuttering, graphics bugging out or not loading correctly. Audio bugs where I lost audio entirely or it kept playing, and speech often did not match the lip syncing and lagged massively behind or was WAY ahead and I'd hear RoboCop talking while I visually saw him standing there awkwardly. There were also a LOT of overlapping audio cues which got worse later in the game. Controller input worked most of the time, but the longer I played (like near the end of it) I had issue after issue with the Xbox controller support. Lot of moments where I was perfectly fine, then the entire thing spazzed out. I had to force quit the game because, at one point, all control (including mouse) stopped working. This only happened one time, but I lost a lot of enjoyment that could've been avoided if the game had been optimized better. Small note: I 100% know the devs are updating the game with hotfixes. I played this a few weeks after it launched, so by the time you read this, all of my complaints may have been fixed so please take this with a grain of salt. The story. I won't go into major spoilers, but there were several issues. Some characters felt like they were forced. Mainly, the bad guy. He feels like he was written to be someone super important to Robo's past but also acts like a stereotypical bad guy. I feel like we were told to both care about his past, but also he is no one special. It's like there was 2 competing ideas on how to handle him that just didn't make sense when you shove them together. The other major character I think was handled better overall, but her stuff left me unsatisfied. Her ending made sense to me, but there were clear missing puzzle pieces here that I felt could've made her story great, if that makes sense. It's like a fast food burger, it got the job done, but it's missing the "homemade" taste and vibe. The story had a stronger start for me, but it went downhill the longer I went on. The bad guy takes WAY too long to finally show up. The flashback sections were overly used and the merc one was downright a waste of time and only seemed to pad the runtime . I think if you got this on a sale and you enjoyed the main game, I would say get this because I know you will find some enjoyment out of this, but I know I am a stickler for story, and after the great job they did with the main game, this just felt like they didn't know what they wanted to do or maybe, there were some major development shift. I can't say what it was, but you can feel how off it is. Still want to see more from this developer and I'd be 100% down for a horror game because they have some devs here with a real good eye for horror scenes, sound design, and visuals. I really think they could make a banger. Overall, I am happy I played it and supported the devs. This one was a bit of a miss for me, but I love the RoboCop movie and it's thanks to the devs that I got to play as him.

input_text: This room escape game adds a clever twist: while solving puzzles and exploring your surroundings, you also have to talk down your captor—and sometimes even enlist their help to escape. Unlike the demo, where nearly everything leaned on AI, the full release uses AI only for dialogue. That means clean visuals, interesting character designs, and cozy environments. It’s still in early access, so expect a few bugs and rough edges. Voice-to-text is clunky (and bafflingly still requires pressing Enter), but overall the game shows ambition. Beyond simply escaping, there are multiple objectives, genuine replayability, and an actual plot tying things together with more depth than you’d expect. The AI integration is a mixed bag. On one hand, it prevents the game from devolving into the demo’s “talk to Catgirl about anime for half an hour, then ask to leave” simplicity. There’s more gameplay, more puzzles, and more structure. On the other, the chatbot often can’t provide new or useful information, especially for trickier puzzles. It’s also far too easy to get characters to like you—idle chatter alone routinely netted me the “best” ending on my first try, which clashes with the progression system that expects players to unlock multiple endings, including bad ones. As it stands, getting to the next story beat sometimes means deliberately tanking your own success, which feels awkward and forced. The “quests” could use more variety. Instead of simply manipulating character affection or replaying scenarios, objectives like cook a meal for Catgirl, drink one of every potion, or offer five different items to the hologram would add depth. Some alternate endings (“escape but sad”) at least offer tougher challenges than the standard “best” ending, which helps balance things. The standout section so far is the space scenario, which recalls other “alone on a space station with an AI” games. Here, the chatbot contributes more meaningfully: providing lore, explaining concepts, and becoming essential to the plot. Paired with stronger puzzles, it feels like it could sustain a game on its own. The problem is replayability—once you know the setup, the AI’s limitations show, especially when the most “AI-like” AI can’t actually guide you in-world. Immersion breaks quickly. Across scenarios, it’s clear the developer is growing. Each one is bigger, more ambitious, and better constructed, steadily evolving from a meme-y proof of concept into something genuinely engaging. The central issue, though, is the gap between what the AI seems to offer and what it actually delivers. A lot of interactions boil down to scripted responses you could just as easily handle with if/then logic, and the illusion of lifelike conversation often collapses into repetitive pantomime. Occasionally the AI smooths over frustrations—like when I couldn’t find a potion ingredient and the Witch just gave me one—but these moments are rare. The dating sim aspects also fall flat compared to even modest visual novels. Relationships progress too quickly, payoff is shallow, and the loop resets with every scenario, leaving no sense of permanence. It’s hard to feel invested when simply flirting a bit unlocks someone’s entire character arc. Replayability ends up feeling more like FACADE: amusing experiments with what you can say, but without real consequences. There are some easter eggs, randomized elements, and cosmetic unlocks, but they don’t meaningfully shake up the experience. And since you can essentially handwave items into existence through dialogue (“I give you X item”), progression feels flimsy. That said, the game succeeds as an exploration of how large language models can fit into gameplay. Used not as a narrative engine, but as a companion, assistant, or knowledge gate, this system shows promise. Imagine a detective noir where the AI plays your spunky assistant, or a survival game where you rely on it for medicine, reminders, or guidance. The tech’s best role may not be as the star, but as the support that makes traditional mechanics richer. I recommend it now as I see it can get better with each update, and there is actual depth of writing and creation behind the LLM facade- unique maps, mechanics, worldbuilding, and drawn art, turning it away from AI cash grab into an attempt at a more immersive experience layered on top of the standard escape room experience. And no microtransactions, some modding support, I'm interested in seeing where this game goes.

I hope to come back in a year to find a bunch more stuff but, even if it hasn't had a lot more added,I feel I've had my money's worth. As for bugs, yes there are some, but I haven't seen anything game breaking and they are actively being squashed -- e.g. within the month or so since I've started playing, some odd drone and conveyor belt behaviour have already been fixed. No crashes in my 96h of play time. You'll see the usual negative reviews making a big fuss of scattered bugs (yes colonists' AI sucks, but that doesn't prevent your progress), or claiming that "devs aren't working" (aren't monthly updates/fixes frequent enough for them?). If I took to heart every negative review from people who expect every game to be live service, I would probably never buy another game again...

input_text: Basically Factorio in a hex grid. But ... early game. No blueprints, no circuit networks, no trains. If you like Factorio and want a 60 hour diversion, this game is a good investment. Note this review is from 8/30/25, the game is pretty new and will change/ Pros: - I like the research: Provide the right ingredients, and research happens. No need to pick the tech. - I like the factories. Provide the needed ingredients, and it will make the thing. No need to pick the recipe. - I like the idea of 6 planes of existence, each which only has 3 of the 6 available elements. This forces adjustment in each plane as options change. - Having power "cables" that can't go underground (at first) forces you to rethink how to wire belts and power. - The overarching idea of entropy entering the planes of existence works. - Magic as a way to provide instant power for early game is a nice shortcut. - While still early, the game never crashed despite several updates. Cons (these are early game issues that will likely be fixed!): - I never could find the Air plane. Maybe it doesn't exist yet? So ... only 5 planes of existence? - When you reload, the gates are reset (no longer open), and random entropy shows up that wasn't there before. I expect these issue will get fixed, but they were annoying. - Entropy and rifts are generally annoying. Early on, you can't close them. So, if they appear in a critical part of your base (they can appear _anywhere_!), you are screwed. Relocate and deal with it! - A spell to clear away entropy also picks up items on belts and puts them in your inventory??? WTH? Why do I want to grab random items while clearly entropy??? This spell changed twice with updates as I played, so I guess it is being tweaked? - The end game goal of building 1000 'things" for each element isn't fun. 1000 is too much, make it 250. Also, give some way of tracking progress so you don't have to go to the gate to see how close you are. And ... why does the gate go past 1000 if you give it more stuff? If there is no point to going past 1000, stop there! - This game needs a wiki! Like ... what is a "chasm?" The game said wind power is better with them ... but I have no idea what they are. Not being able to find the air plane might be related, but I can't tell. And ... how many items per second do belts carry? That would be nice to know.

input_text: After compelteing 100% of F1 manager 2024, would I recommend it? Disappointingly no. Now dont get me wrong this game has its positives, to start with it looks and sounds fantastic. Being not only fully licensed letting the real world of F1 be shown it also has audio snippets from the real drivers and crew members that give the game that little bit of life. On top of that although the game had a rough launch it has since been updated and made a stable and rather bug free experience. But unfortunately that doesn't distract from what I feel is poor gameplay. In terms of mid race planning and management the game is fine, the choices you make are no different that the other motorsport games you can pick up and play, however outside the racing I feel that there is too much of a focus on its real world comparisons and metrics rather than the gameplay being fun and understandable. There are so many systems that are too focused on accuracy that it takes away from the games feel. What I mean is shown in areas such as the part development where the game tends to show the specific metrics and how they are measured rather than just showing how it would affect the car and I feel this is a case of detail getting in the way of a game just being fun. The trend of the game being extremely detail oriented wouldn't be a issue if the game itself warranted it, but it forces you to learn and adjust to all the nitty gritty details of a F1 car and team and then the game itself is extremely easy to beat even when set to be realistic. Team fluctuate in performance way too much way too quickly, drivers make nonsensical moves and your targets are either way to easy to achieve or it's impossible to keep your job with again little to no sense being made by why they are the way they are. This is a type of game im quite familiar with having played hundreds of hours of motorsport manager, and having 100%'ed the previous 2 F1 manager games which I'm not reviewing retrospectively due to them having the same issue as this one does. And due to myself really enjoying management styled games I was wanting something I could sink my teeth into and waste hours upon hours playing and I just couldn't gel with it. Its as if its trying to be compared to the football manager series of games but with just surface level detail and no depth to what it means. and that makes the gameplay loop unsatisfying to be a part of. Motorsport manager has a less detailed and less impressive look and feel to the graphics and audio, it lacks the licencing meaning they use rip-off named parodies of the teams and drivers, and bends the rules to include mechanics such as promotion and demotion between the leagues of racing, so its far from a simulation of the F1 world, but its so much more fun as a game, which to me is more important. It has the depth of a true management game while still keeping the simplicity to help people who are not F1 mad adjust to the game. As a completionist the game has the expected challenges such as winning the championships, winning certain types of races, performing the general actions such as signing a driver as well as some more specific challenges such as having one of your drivers become the youngest world champion, winning all three championships at once (Driver, team and pit stop) and getting both drivers to a 100% setup at any race weekend. At launch some of these were bugged and unable to be obtained but to my knowledge these issues have been fixed. Its not really a impressive game to hunt, and depending on how much you focus just playing it for the certain achievements it also might end up being a rather large time sink and a boring one too as you might have won multiple championships but need to keep changing drivers while still keeping on top to try and get the youngest title as a example. Overall id give the game a 3/10, Unless you are a avid F1 fan, who can look past the almost fake complex mechanics to play a casual and easy management game I'd skip this. If you instead are able to look past the game needing the right names of teams I would recommend getting motorsport manager as to me its a much more rewarding, interesting and fun example of this style of game.

input_text: Clean, satisfying WWII turn based tactics on superb maps 195 hours on record The Troop is a clean, satisfying WWII turn based tactics game, set on detailed and well-crafted battle maps. Visuals are surprisingly tasty when zoomed in, the tutorial gets you fighting fast, and the campaign plus historical scenarios offer plenty of variety with smooth, trouble free gameplay. Gameplay & Mechanics [] Tactical feel: Alternating turns with clear objectives, positioning, line-of-sight, smoke, terrain and cover all matter. [] Unit identity: Infantry, armour and artillery feel distinct, flanking and combined arms are rewarded. [] Flow: No steep learning curve and the tutorial gets you moving quickly. [] Scenarios: A decent campaign, solid skirmishes, and story scenarios based on historical actions keep things fresh. [] Maps: Varied, readable battlefields that make tactical choices obvious at a glance. [] Replay value:[ Objectives and starting positions invite replays to test different plans and strategies. Performance & Stability (195 hours) Stability: Gameplay is smooth and trouble free, no crashes or glitches in my experience. Graphics & Sound [] Visuals: Surprisingly detailed up close, vehicles, buildings and props have individuality and nice touches. I love when machine gun rounds ricochet off armour and streak into the camera. [] Audio: Functional rather than cinematic, weapons and explosions land, but the overall mix is fairly basic. Verdict The Troop nails the sweet spot: accessible, tactically satisfying and quietly handsome. It scratches that WWII itch and, after 195 hours, I still replay scenarios to try new approaches. Easy recommend.

input_text: I like the game, but there some serious annoyances. First the good. I love how the exploration ships are used for more than just exploration. That idea alone is brilliant. The thought of purchasing your war ships through private companies and performing research through those companies is a great idea, but I do not feel it was implemented well. Perhaps if each company specialized in something or gave you a patented technology that only they could provide, or some incentive to pick one company over the other then it would be outstanding. The game has that "Just one more turn" feeling to it, I did find myself wanting to see how something would improve my situation once it was finished being (built or researched). That is pretty much the end of the good for me. When I first read the description of the game where it described how you have to use media against your enemies and for your friends, I thought that is a great idea. Unfortunately, it is horribly implemented in this game. First the concept of how it works is pretty vague. I pictured it my mind that I would run some negative propaganda against my foe, and he would do the same and a short while later we would be at war, but the reality is the opposite. In my game every time I ran negative media against someone, they responded with positive media, which pretty much negates my negative media, which ends in neither of us going to war. As a sidenote, I find it ironically funny that I can run a propaganda item that says my enemy has been crossing our border illegally, but I can't actually cross my enemies border to attempt to start a war because we are not at war. Unfortunately, I was unable to experience any combat in my game as I could not declare war on anyone and could not start a war no matter how hard I tried. The media idea needs to be rethought in my opinion, or just scrapped all together. If there is one good thing about the media portion of the game it is that you can influence your own population to provide research bonuses, or defense bonuses, etc. Five races seems to be a bit slim, perhaps the developer is planning on adding more in an expansion pack. It seems to be pretty stable, I did not run into any gameplay issues, no crashes. I really hope the developer can make the game better, there are some great ideas here, but I feel it just needs more playtesting to iron out the wrinkles in the gameplay.

input_text: First Steam review, as this game came out yesterday and I figure it'd be helpful. As of right now - it's a mobile game. 100MBs of bright colours. But, is that a bad thing? No. Pros: - Seemingly no bugs or major issues, as there often are with early access games. - Very user-friendly tutorial - I learned all I needed to know quickly and efficiently and was able to practice the new skills. Not too repetitive. - Can already smell a "addictive" game coming along, seeing as I haven't really stopped other than to write this. - A lot of potential for growth, edits, mods, etc like Civ - Could play it on a potato. - Designed like Angry Birds - level by level. Can't really get bored of doing the same thing, as you get new tasks every level, whether that means making $3m before anyone else or strictly winning. - Low price, so if you don't like it, it's not a big deal Cons: - Must follow the storyline - no skirmish mode (yet), although this could turn into a Civ-style game. Give it a year. - Basic things like volume control, ability to window the game, etc are not implemented - No caps on the percentages. When upgrade costs are 250% but Influence is 30%, good luck playing at all. - Easy mode is still very difficult Small bug - The first level that is not a tutorial, you're tasked with making $1m before your counterpart. Mine, Joe, was at 981k - and I was stuck at 854k as i was too click-happy with upgrades. Impulsively, I got a loan of $154k, and beat Joe... I feel that's not supposed to happen. Maybe make it so that you must pay off all loans before winning? We'll leave it at that for now. Devs, if you're seeing this, good luck on your adventure!

input_text: First things first: This is a thumbs up because the game does nothing really wrong - it also isn't great at anything. Consider it a 51%, it passes base. That aside, this is a generic, derivative time management game, with very mediocre visuals and a completely forgetable (and thankfully skipable) story. The attempts at humour were on the childish side for me, but the voice over was actually competent, a surprise for a game of this budget. The music and sound design are also competent, as in: repetitive but not horrible. As for the customization of the protagonists, it consists of hats and skins that you get as rewards, so... meh? On the positive side: No bugs or crashes. This will likely run on a potato. Gameplay-wise, I found it way too easy for my tastes and very light on strategy. The level design is, you guessed it, competent enough, but not really interesting. It took no effort at all to finish all levels with gold stars, so if you're looking for something relaxing, this will maybe work for you. A little bit of planning and strategy will also allow you to beat most developers' times - which by the way is only necessary once for the achievement, making this an easy game to 100%. All in all, it's alright, I guess. Competent enough is not a great recommendation I realize, but it's not a bad game for casual time management fans. Just wait for a sale.

input_text: After the amount of hours I have spent in the game, I feel legit to give an honest review about it. I had FPS experience before I started to play PS2, mostly just casual gaming with various titles from the genre. Sadly I got spoiled too much of the scale that it is difficult to go back on those. The only reason I will play other FPS games too is to have more competitive and very controlled environment to try out own reaction times and skills in well known titles. If you are expecting very polished and smooth experience with always balanced and fun fights, then PS2 might not be for you. There has been ups and downs during the game's life time, but dev team has done their best to keep the players satisfied. At this point I want to say that put the game already to download, because it takes a while, unless you have limited data plan or small storage. Otherwise there is no reason to try out, except if you are easily addicted or do have unsupported operating system. Some of the older computers will have performance issues, but my oldish rig is doing fine with competitive performance. What can you expect from the game: You will die, many times, all the time. There are people who have been playing this game since beta and they know every minor detail of their favourite weapons and good locations to kill you. But don't worry, there are also same people in your team, who will probably save you before you get in danger zone. Game has cross faction textual chat for the area you are fighting, so expect to see people cursing how sad other team is by bringing too many players in the fight to break the population balance. Some people don't have legs so they just sit in their vehicles all the time and try to shoot infantry with easy to kill cannons if they aren't in real danger. Maps are quite huge, but usually the killer is hiding nearby even when the shot comes out of nowhere. According the chat many people have RTS background, specially from StarCraft and from zerg faction. You can play alone or be part of a squad of 12 players, which can be part of platoon of four squads, which can be part of some outfit public operations to run multiple platoons. Depending the situations you are alone or there are 96+ friendlies with you in same fight. There are no matchmaking or any custom game etc. You are in your character in one of the five servers, in one of the four continents (not counting Koltyr the new player training "continent"), in one of the many bases. There will or won't be enemies or friendlies, but you have all the right be in there. It is very confusing at the first, because shots coming from all over the place or from nowhere. There is an in-game map, which you can use to navigate in the fights (think as joining a match). You can get all the stuff with the in-game currency you get by playing the game. Only the swag and character vanity are restricted to DBC, which you get only with real money. Weapons are "sidegrades" so that they specialize in certain roles, like gaining firerate by losing damage, etc. You might get fully upgraded vehicles with swag from veteran players if you ask kindly. There is no Pay-to-win, but you can buy XP boosts and premium membership to get more value out of your in-game actions, which will make your cert (in-game currency) gain faster. Also paying players might have squad boosts, which will affect to other players in the group, so F2P players can get extra XP boost without paying. There are three different factions, that have different style of weaponry. For new players some might be easier to start with, because more controllable, but over the time it is just personal preference which backstory you want to support. Spandex babes, teamkilling blueberries or oppressive internationalists. Community can send own cosmetic creation to player studio to get them in game. There is no PC-PS4 realm, so can't show the PC master race dominion to console plebs. (/s) TL;DR: Gud gaem, not ded gaem, not P2W, crying redditors, nice content creators, Player studio <3<3
